title: Sharing the merit
hook: ending practice by dedicating whatever good was done to all beings

segments.voice: Yesterday, candle and incense: light for wisdom, scent for good conduct that travels against the wind. Your line was light and scent. Did you light a candle? Day one hundred forty-three.

At the end of a Buddhist ceremony in Thailand, something small happens that visitors often miss. While the monks chant, people slowly pour water from a little vessel into a bowl, a thin, steady stream, until the chant ends. Some hold a finger under the stream. Afterward, the water is often poured out at the foot of a tree. It looks like cleaning up. It isn't. It's the last and, many Buddhists would say, one of the most beautiful parts of practice: giving away the good you've just done.
screen: `A THIN STREAM OF WATER.` → `POURED AT THE FOOT OF A TREE.` → `GIVING AWAY THE GOOD.`

segments.voice: The Pali word is punna, usually translated merit. It means the goodness that comes from good actions: giving, keeping the precepts, meditating. You'd think the natural thing is to keep it. But Buddhists across traditions end practice by sharing it. In Theravada, this is called pattidana, the giving of merit. The oldest roots are in a short text called the discourse outside the walls. It pictures dead relatives waiting outside the walls of their old home, hoping someone will remember them. When the living give food to monks and dedicate the gift, the text says the relatives can rejoice in it and be helped. The line people still chant is idam vo natinam hotu: may this be for our relatives. That's what the water pouring is. Many chants that go with it compare the merit to rivers filling the ocean. And the person who hears about your good deed and says sadhu, well done, is sharing it by rejoicing. In Mahayana traditions, the dedication goes wider still. At the end of a sitting or a chant, practitioners dedicate the merit to the awakening of all beings, everywhere, without exception. Yesterday's candle comes back here, because teachers often explain the logic with one. When you light another candle from yours, your flame doesn't get smaller. The room just gets brighter. Merit shared isn't merit lost. There's also a quiet effect on the one who shares. Ending with a dedication keeps practice from becoming a private savings account. You sat, you gave, you kept a precept, and then you open your hands again. The good doesn't stop at you.
screen: `PUNNA: THE GOOD FROM GOOD ACTIONS.` · `RELATIVES OUTSIDE THE WALLS.` · `DEDICATED TO ALL BEINGS.` · `ONE CANDLE LIGHTS ANOTHER.` · then, large: `MAY IT BE SHARED.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath settle. Rest for a while in the sitting itself. Then, near the end, bring to mind whatever good came from this practice: a little calm, a little kindness, a little clarity. Picture it as water in a small cup. Now picture pouring it out, a thin, steady stream flowing on to others: someone you love, someone you've lost, a stranger, all beings. If you'd like, use the old words, idam vo natinam hotu, may this be for our relatives. Or simply open your hands. The bell holds the time.
Sharing the merit. Ending practice by dedicating whatever good was done to others, and to all beings, like water poured out until it reaches the sea.
Your line: may it be shared. Today, dedicate today's sitting to someone else. And when someone does something good, say well done, and share it by rejoicing. Day one hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Buddhists across traditions end ceremonies and meditation by dedicating the merit to others; in Theravada countries this is often done by pouring water while monks chant, and in Mahayana traditions with a dedication to the awakening of all beings.

fork.reveal: practice traditionally ends with a dedication: whatever good was done is shared, with relatives, with all beings.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhists collect merit like points.
what it means: practice ends by giving the good away, dedicated to others.

what a scholar hears: the Tirokudda Sutta (Khuddakapatha 7) is a canonical root of merit dedication for departed relatives, and the Mahayana widened it to parinamana, dedication to all beings' awakening.

notes: The Pali 'idam vo natinam hotu' (Tirokudda Sutta) is given without diacritics; confirm spelling (idaṃ vo ñātīnaṃ hotu).
The water-pouring chant comparing merit to rivers filling the ocean ('yatha varivaha pura…') is paraphrased; confirm.
The candle simile is described as how teachers often explain sharing merit, not as canonical.
Water poured at the foot of a tree after the ceremony is a common Thai custom; confirm.
